lead: Two pictures of love that holds nothing back. Paul, unable to bear the separation any longer, gives up the company of Timothy and sends him to strengthen the young church of Thessalonica in its trials. In the Temple a poor widow puts in two small coins, “everything she had”, and Jesus calls his disciples to look at her. The key words are strengthen and everything.

r.h: We sent Timothy to strengthen you
set: Paul had been forced to leave Thessalonica after only a short stay (Acts 17:10). He went on to Beroea and then to Athens (Acts 17:10–15). From Athens, worried about the new believers he had left behind in the middle of persecution, he sent Timothy back to them. Our passage tells of that decision; a few verses later Timothy returns with good news of their faith and love (3:6). Acts tells the movements of Paul's companions more briefly, and the two accounts are usually fitted together without difficulty.
str: vv. 1–2: Paul stays alone in Athens and sends Timothy.
vv. 3–4: persecution was to be expected; Paul had warned them.
v. 5: his fear that the tempter had undone his work.
kw: To make firm, to set on a solid base. Jesus gives Peter the same task: “strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). Strengthening the faith of others is the work of every apostle and pastor.

Literally pressure, being pressed hard. Paul uses it often for the troubles that come with following Christ. He does not promise the Thessalonians that faith will spare them; he tells them that it is “what we are destined for”.
The name Matthew gives to the devil in the desert (Matthew 4:3). Paul sees in persecution not only human hostility but a spiritual attack on faith.
vv: Therefore when we could bear it no longer, we decided to be left alone in Athens;

A few verses earlier Paul said that being separated from them made him feel “orphaned” (2:17, literally). Now he chooses to be left alone for their sake. He feels the absence of his converts as a parent feels the absence of children (see 2:7, 11).
and we sent Timothy, our brother and co-worker for God in proclaiming the gospel of Christ, to strengthen and encourage you for the sake of your faith,
Timothy was still young (1 Timothy 4:12), but Paul calls him “co-worker for God”. Some manuscripts have “servant of God”; the NRSV follows the more daring reading.
so that no one would be shaken by these persecutions.
The Greek verb for “shaken” was used of a dog wagging its tail, and so of being flattered or unsettled. Paul fears not only fear itself but being drawn away gently.
I was afraid that somehow the tempter had tempted you and that our labor had been in vain.
Even the great apostle knew anxiety for his people. Pastoral love includes worry, and it turns worry into action: he sends help.
ch: Paul and Barnabas told the first converts the same thing: “It is through many persecutions that we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:22). The Church sees in Paul's sending of Timothy the pattern of all pastoral care: the shepherd does not abandon the flock in danger but sends help and seeks news. Today too there are Christians in many lands who suffer for their faith. We pray for them, that no one be shaken, and for those who wrong them.

r.h: She put in everything she had
set: Jesus is teaching in the Temple in the last days before his passion. Just before this scene he warns against scribes who “devour widows’ houses and for the sake of appearance say long prayers” (12:40). Just after it, he foretells that the Temple itself will be thrown down (13:1–2). The widow stands between those two sayings.

The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, where anyone could go. Later Jewish tradition, written down in the Mishnah, speaks of thirteen trumpet-shaped chests for offerings there. Mark explains the widow's coins for readers who used Roman money, which fits the early tradition that he wrote for the Church in Rome.
str: v. 41: Jesus sits and watches the giving; the rich give much.
v. 42: the widow's two small coins.
vv. 43–44: Jesus calls the disciples and teaches them what he has seen.
kw: two small copper coins, which are worth a penny
The lepton was the smallest coin in use. Two of them made a Roman quadrans, a quarter of the Roman as, itself a small copper coin. In money it was almost nothing.
The rich gave from what they had left over; she gave from what she lacked. Jesus measures a gift not by its size but by what it costs.
all she had to live on
Bios means both life and the means of life. She put in, literally, “her whole life”. A few days later Jesus will give his whole life.
vv: He sat down opposite the treasury, and watched the crowd putting money into the treasury.
Jesus watches how people give. Nothing done for God is unseen by him, however small.
A poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which are worth a penny.
She could have kept one coin. She gave both.
Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the treasury.
“Truly I tell you” marks a solemn teaching. Jesus calls his disciples especially to hear it, for they will be the shepherds of the Church.
but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.

Many commentators also hear a note of sorrow: the system that took her last coin is the same one Jesus has just criticized for devouring widows' houses. The Church's reading has always been above all a praise of her total trust in God.
ch: The Catechism, speaking of poverty of heart, recalls that shortly before his passion Jesus gave his disciples the example of the poor widow of Jerusalem who out of her poverty put in all she had to live on (CCC 2544). She has become the image of every hidden gift: the small offering in the church box, the time given by those who have little time, the prayer of the sick who have nothing else to give. The widow gives two coins; Christ gives himself, and in the Holy Qurbono we offer our small gifts together with his perfect one.

qa: Does this mean that the poor should give away their last money?

No. Jesus does not lay a rule on the poor; he reveals what God sees. The Church also teaches that justice demands care for widows and the poor (James 1:27), and Jesus has just condemned those who exploit them. The lesson is for everyone: God values a gift by the love and trust it carries, and he who gives everything to God is never forgotten by him.
study: Do I give to God from what I have left over, or from what it costs me?
Who in my parish or family needs a “Timothy” sent to strengthen them this week, and could I be that person?
